Arthur |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PrtHDwAAQBAJ&dq=abraham+arthur+gottlieb&pg=PT4 |title=Developments in Lymphoid Cell Biology |date=2018-01-18 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-1-351-08824-4 |language=en}}</ref> (December 14, 1937 – June 7, 1998) was an American biologist and [[Immunology|immunologist]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Saxon |first=Wolfgang |date=1998-06-09 |title=Arthur Gottlieb, 60, Biologist-Immunologist and Company Founder |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/06/09/us/arthur-gottlieb-60-biologist-immunologist-and-company-founder.html |access-date=2022-07-04 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Gottlieb was born in [[Haifa]] under the [[Mandatory Palestine|British Mandate]] on December 14, 1937, to an American mother and a British father, who was then deputy minister of agriculture under the British Mandate. He grew up with his mother who returned to New York when he was 13 months old. Gottlieb attended the [[Bronx High School of Science]] with the class of 1954.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=A. Arthur Gottlieb |url=https://c250.columbia.edu/c250_celebrates/your_columbians/arthur_gottlieb.html |access-date=2022-07-04 |website=c250.columbia.edu|last=Gottlieb|first=Marise|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241213192418/https://c250.columbia.edu/c250_celebrates/your_columbians/arthur_gottlieb.html|archive-date=13 December 2024|url-status=live}}</ref> He entered [[Columbia College (New York)|Columbia College]] in 1953 under the early admission scholarship program by [[Ford Foundation]].<ref name=":0" /> He was a coxswain for Columbia's rowing team and graduated from Columbia in 1957, [[Phi Beta Kappa|phi beta kappa]].<ref name=":1" />

Gottlieb received his medical degree from [[New York University School of Medicine]] with the highest class standing and did his medical internship and residency at [[Peter Bent Brigham Hospital]] in [[Boston]]. He worked in the [[National Heart Institute]] while serving in the [[United States Public Health Service]] and became a faculty member at [[Harvard Medical School]] in 1968. He became a tenured professor at [[Rutgers University]] in 1972 before joining the faculty of [[Tulane Medical School]] in 1975 as chairman of the Department of Microbiology and Immunology and professor of Medicine for 23 years until his death in 1998.<ref name=":1" />

Gottlieb's research has focused on the linkages between the neuroendocrine system and the immune system.<ref name=":0" /> He was also the founder and chief executive of Imreg Inc., a company he founded to search for new substances that bolster the human immune system.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |date=June 9, 1998 |title=Dr. Arthur Gottlieb, Aids Researcher |url=http://files.usgwarchives.net/la/orleans/newspapers/00000411.txt |access-date=July 4, 2022 |website=The Times-Picayune}}</ref> He was a fellow of the [[American College of Physicians]] and the [[American Academy of Microbiology]].<ref name=":2" />

In 1987, Gottlieb carried out tests on the body fluid and tissue samples of a deceased St. Louis teenager, showing that AIDS was present in the United States as early as 1969, a decade before the disease was believed to have existed in this country.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1969 Case Shakes Theories of AIDS Origin |url=https://apnews.com/article/ae5ea4cbc41220767c37d4abbe9b85a0 |access-date=2022-07-04 |website=AP NEWS |language=en|date=26 October 1987|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221109160335/https://apnews.com/article/ae5ea4cbc41220767c37d4abbe9b85a0|archive-date=9 November 2022|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Gottlieb died on June 7, 1998, in [[New Orleans]] at age 60.<ref name=":0" />
